Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette:
Tane is a 56-year-old Māori American detective who came to treatment after years of telling himself that whatever happened in childhood was long over and should have stayed there. He grew up with a caregiver whose physical abuse was unpredictable and frighteningly intimate. What remains clearest to him is not a neat story he can tell from beginning to end, but moments that still feel as if they are happening now: the sudden presence of an adult body too close to his, the sense of being trapped, and a burnt smell in the air that seemed to fuse with fear. When he tries to explain the abuse out loud, he often starts firmly and then loses the thread, stopping mid-sentence with his jaw tight and his hands clenched, as if the memory fragments faster than he can organize them. What comes through most strongly then is rage. He says he can go from trying to describe one scene to feeling a violent surge of anger in his body before he has even found the words.

In the years afterward, Tane built a life around competence and control. He became a detective, a role that fit the part of him that believed danger was always near and that survival depended on noticing what other people missed. Even now, he is superalert in ways colleagues experience as thoroughness and intensity. He scans rooms automatically, tracks exits, notices movements in peripheral vision, and has difficulty settling at night because some part of him insists he needs to stay alert. Falling asleep feels like letting his guard down. He lies in bed listening for sounds in the house and checking the air, his body keyed up long after he wants rest.

The reminders that catch him are often humiliating in their speed. A burnt smell—toast left too long in a break-room toaster, scorched coffee, something singed from a street vendor’s grill—can bring back the full memory without warning. His body reacts before he can think: chest tight, stomach dropping, skin hot, muscles braced as if impact is imminent. He has also noticed that certain people unsettle him immediately when they resemble the victims he encounters in his work. On cases involving abuse, if someone’s face, size, posture, or expression echoes those victims in just the wrong way, he feels himself pulled out of the present and flooded with the old memory. Because he works in investigations, these moments are not rare abstractions; they happen in interview rooms, on scene visits, in hospital corridors, in photographs spread across a desk.

Over time he has narrowed his life in practical ways that make sense to him. He avoids other people when he can, not because he thinks of himself as shy, but because contact feels effortful and unpredictable. Since his divorce, that withdrawal has become more pronounced. Outside work he keeps to himself, declines invitations, and leaves social situations early. He also avoids wearing clothes that resemble what he associates with the abuse. He does this with little ceremony—setting shirts back on the rack, discarding items, choosing alternatives quickly—but with a private certainty that certain fabrics or styles are simply not tolerable on his body.

When memories come, he tries to detach from them, to go numb and distant until the wave passes. He describes it as stepping away internally, as if he can watch from somewhere else and not fully be there. Yet this strategy has left him feeling cut off even in moments that should be good. One of the more confusing features for him is that positive emotion itself can become unsettling. If he begins to feel warmth, pride, closeness, or enjoyment, he often stiffens, suspicious of it, as though feeling good makes him vulnerable or means he has missed something dangerous. He does not present this as a theory so much as a lived alarm: when things seem safe, he trusts himself less.

Tane has come to believe that the abuse ruined his understanding of how the world works. He says, with a flat conviction, that whatever ideas he once had about adults protecting children or life having any basic fairness were shattered long ago. He is harshest with himself. The persistence of his reactions has become proof, in his mind, that he is a lousy coper. He compares himself unfavorably to an imagined person who would have mastered this by now, and he carries a deeper, older conclusion that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he is. He knows how severe that sounds when said aloud, but he does not say it for effect; it is one of the beliefs that has sat with him the longest.

He finally sought help after a recent cluster of reminders at work and at home left him feeling less able to contain things in the ways he usually does. He noticed he was sleeping even less, avoiding more people, and struggling to speak coherently when he tried to tell any part of his story. What frightened him most was not only the force of the reactions, but the possibility that this was simply his character laid bare. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to become a different man, but to be able to sleep, to stay present when reminders hit, and to feel something good without immediately going on guard.
